_comment: WHAT SHOULD BE TRUE ABOUT YOUR SYSTEM.
You own this file. The watchdog READS it and never edits it: a system that
can relax its own expectations has none. Weakening a check here is a
decision, made deliberately, by you.
The watchdog compares each expectation against what is actually true and
reports the difference. It does not fix anything. A watchdog that repairs
what it finds stops being a measurement and becomes another writer nobody
is watching.
WHY THIS EXISTS. An automated system fails silently by default. Every run
exits cleanly whether it produced everything or nothing, because producing
nothing is not an error: it is a successful run of a thing that found
nothing to do. A long run of those looks, from every log and every exit
code, exactly like a system working perfectly. One person working alone has
no colleague to lean over and say that looks wrong.
WRITING YOUR OWN. A check that is green the day you write it is checking
something that was never going to break. Write checks against things you
have seen go wrong, and against things whose failure you would not notice.
The second kind matters more.
Each entry needs an id, a severity, what you expect in plain words, why it
is here, and the conditions under which it would go red. If the id is not
one the watchdog knows how to check, it will tell you so rather than
quietly passing.

checks.why: This is the one that catches a system which runs, exits cleanly and does nothing. No other check here would notice, because every other check is perfectly happy with a system that has stopped.
checks.red_when: capture breaks, a source changes shape, or a credential expires. All three fail quietly and none of them produce an error.

checks.expect: every person has the identifier you chose in Layer 2
checks.why: A record with no identifier cannot be matched, held, or counted. It is a name in a folder.
checks.red_when: records are created by hand, or imported from a source that did not carry the identifier.

checks.expect: no two records share one identifier
checks.why: Two records for one person means two half-histories and no way to tell which is right. Everything above Layer 2 assumes this holds.
checks.red_when: the same person arrives from two sources under two spellings of their name.

checks.expect: most events can be attributed to somebody
checks.why: An event nobody can attribute is history the system cannot use. A pile of them means a source is producing events about people who are not in your records.
checks.red_when: a new source is connected before the people it talks about exist as records.

checks.expect: nobody you picked up by hand appears on the daily page
checks.why: The hold exists to stop the system acting on a conversation you took over. A held person on the action list defeats it completely, and the failure is invisible unless something looks.
checks.red_when: a hold is recorded under an identifier the ordering does not check.

checks.expect: every hold has something more precise than a name attached
checks.why: A check matches what it is given. A hold recorded under a bare name is invisible to anything holding only a link, and a name-only hold cannot tell two people apart.
checks.red_when: a hold is added by hand, or by a source that only knew the person's name.

checks.expect: no code writes straight over a file in your CRM
checks.why: Opening a file for writing empties it before a single byte of the new content arrives. If anything goes wrong in between, the old content is gone and there is no copy.
checks.red_when: somebody adds a quick script. It is always a quick script.
